newsitem.title: CHINA: China backs stock warning with tough penalties.
newsitem.headline: China backs stock warning with tough penalties.

text.p: China confirmed on Friday that it had replaced the chief of its top stock market watchdog amid a series of tough measures aimed at curbing improper trading.
However, the latest moves to cool China's surging markets had little impact on Friday with stocks closing sharply higher.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) said after the markets closed that Zhou Zhengqing, chairman of the Securities Commission under the State Council, or cabinet, had taken up an additional job as head of the market watchdog.
Zhou Daojiong had been serving as head of the CSRC but securities industry sources said last month he had been replaced because he was seen as too soft in reining in China's unruly stock markets.
China late on Thursday levied tough penalties against banks and brokerages for speculative trading.
But share indices closed up sharply on Friday, and brokers said the test would come next week when the market has a chance to react to the top level shake-up in the securities industry.
They said trading would remain cautious in the near term, but sharp falls were unlikely on Monday as the news about the change at the top of the CSRC had been expected.

After the markets closed on Thursday, China punished Shenzhen Development Bank, the key blue chip on the southern bourse in Shenzhen, by sacking its president and seizing 90 million yuan ($10.8 million) in bank profits from trading in its own shares.
Beijing also dismissed the head of the Shanghai branch of the state-run Industrial and Commercial Bank of China for providing loans to securities companies for stock speculation.
The heads of three major securities firms were fired for speculating in stocks.
"This shows the authorities are cracking down on securities-related crimes as hard as on other crimes," said a broker at China Guotai Securities in Shenzhen.
Shanghai and Shenzhen A shares for domestic investors fell sharply at the opening of trade on Friday but closed higher.
In Shanghai, the A share index gained 33.084 points or 2.61 percent to close at 1,298.922, while the foreign currency B share index added 1.013 points or 1.22 percent to 83.931.
In Shenzhen, the A share index powered up 18.18 points or 4.40 percent to end at 431.09 after opening down 5.67 percent. The B share index gained 2.84 points or 1.98 percent to 146.16.
The punitive measures followed last week's government ban on state banks speculating in the stock markets, and earlier moves to stop state companies and listed firms from such activities.
China has been trying to limit risk to the banking system by keeping bank funds out of its speculative stock markets.
Brokers said small retail investors and some institutions were still keen to buy and some people took the early sell-off on Friday as an opportunity to pick up shares cheaply.
"The market has been aware of it (the punishments) for some time, so investors thought they might as well do a little bottom fishing," said one analyst at a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
However, the stock markets were expected to continue weak in the short term as state banks unwind their positions.
The threat of a further crackdown if share prices move up too sharply will cap the markets and keep prices within a narrow range through July, brokers said.
Before Beijing announced its measures to check speculation, many investors bought on expectations prices would climb before China recovers the British colony of Hong Kong on July 1.
Many had believed that Beijing would not want to risk political embarrassment with a clampdown on the domestic market ahead of the transfer of power.
Government regulators defied market expectations by starting their campaign to rein in prices in May.
